hypothesis: Who the household is (demographics) and when the snapshot is (calendar) predict 4-week spend.
transformation_description: Baseline: demographic codes, has_demographics, snapshot day index, week-of-year.

hypothesis: A household's recent purchasing behaviour (spend in trailing windows, trip frequency, recency, trend) predicts its next-4-week spend; history features dominate demographics.
transformation_description: Added transaction-history features: spend in 28/56/84/112/364-day windows, trip counts, days since last trip, active days, recent-vs-prior trend, avg basket value, lifetime spend/days, quantity, discounts, store count, snapshot calendar.
reasoning_summary: Future spend is highly autocorrelated; trailing spend and trip frequency should far outperform demographics alone.

hypothesis: Beyond raw trailing spend, WHAT a household buys (department mix, brand, basket composition, unit price) and HOW it shops (timing, store loyalty, discount use) carry extra signal about future 4-week spend.
transformation_description: Added product-mix features (top-10 department spend shares, national-brand share, unit price, basket size/lines, store concentration, weekend/evening timing, discount shares) and more spend windows (14/182) plus lag-1-year spend on top of E001.
reasoning_summary: Department mix and basket composition capture household type and price tier that raw spend totals miss; more spend windows and dynamics help the model separate stable shoppers from spiky ones.

hypothesis: Marketing exposure (campaigns targeted, coupon redemptions) and household demographics (with interactions of recent spend with demographics and seasonality) improve prediction of future 4-week spend beyond E002's history+mix features.
transformation_description: Added n_campaigns by type, recent campaign count, coupon redemption counts/recency; demographic ordinal codes; interactions spend_28×age/size/kids/season/homeowner/tenure.
reasoning_summary: Campaign targeting and coupon use plausibly drive near-term purchases, and demographics shift the spend level a given trailing history implies; seasonality interactions let the spend-to-future mapping vary over the year.

hypothesis: Marketing exposure (campaign targeting by type and recency, coupon redemption counts/recency) and household demographics (ordinal age/size/income/homeowner/kids codes) add predictive signal for future 4-week spend beyond transaction history and product mix, and interact with recent spend.
transformation_description: Added to E002: campaign counts (total, by TypeA/B/C, recent-84d), coupon redemption counts/recency, ordinal demographic codes + class2 category, and two interaction terms (campA×spend_28, campaigns×has_demo). All built via groupby aggregations to avoid the duplicate-row bug that killed E003.
reasoning_summary: Campaign targeting and coupon use are direct retailer signals of engagement that should correlate with near-term purchasing; demographics capture household size/lifecycle that scales spend. E003 tested this but failed on a merge bug, so the hypothesis is still untested.

hypothesis: Recency-weighted (exponentially decayed) spend rate, weekly spend level/variability, and long-run average weekly spend predict future 4-week spend better than fixed trailing-window sums alone.
transformation_description: Added to E004: exp-decayed spend (halflife 14/28/56/112), window ratios, same-window-last-year spend, weekly spend stats (mean/std/max/active share/zero-streak/12-wk slope), total spend & avg weekly all-time, spend in current partial week.
reasoning_summary: Decayed spend captures both level and recency of purchasing in one feature; weekly stats and long-run averages capture household baseline and churn, which trailing-window sums miss.

hypothesis: The target's zero-inflation structure is still under-modeled: whether a household buys in the next 4 weeks depends on its inter-purchase gap structure and normalized recency, not just trailing spend. Explicit gap statistics, active-week counts, recency×rate interactions, and extra decay halflives (7/224d) will sharpen prediction of both the zero and the amount.
transformation_description: Added to E005: inter-purchase gap mean/max/std (112d), 28d zero-block share (364d), active-week counts (4/26/52w), trip counts (14/112/182d), last-basket value, recency normalized by gap mean, recency×rate84 and no-trip×rate interactions, extra exp decays (hl=7, 224).
reasoning_summary: Zero-inflated targets are driven by whether a household shops at all; gap structure and normalized recency capture that better than raw trailing spend, and interactions let the model combine "likely to shop" with "how much when they do".

hypothesis: The target is autoregressive on aligned 28-day blocks: future_spend_4w at snapshot s−28 is exactly spend in [s−27, s], which is fully observable at snapshot s. Adding these aligned lag features (lag1..lag4, same-window-last-year, trend/ratio/mean/std of the lag series) lets the model express target-vs-target dynamics that cumulative trailing windows cannot.
transformation_description: Added to E006: aligned-block lag features lag1..lag4 (spend in [s−27,s], [s−55,s−28], [s−83,s−56], [s−111,s−84]), same-window-last-year spend, lag trend/ratio, 4-lag mean and std, and last-year ratio.
reasoning_summary: The previous snapshot's target is exactly computable at the current snapshot, giving a perfectly aligned autoregressive series that cumulative-window features cannot represent; this should sharpen predictions for both active and zero-spend households.

hypothesis: Spend features are heavy-tailed (max ~26k vs median ~74 target); a model on raw dollars over-weights extreme households. Log1p-transforming large non-negative spend/count features (keeping ratios, shares, codes, calendar terms raw) improves validation MAE.
transformation_description: log1p on 21 heavy-tailed non-negative columns of E006 (spend windows, decayed spend, weekly stats, tenure, life_spend, total_spend, z-decay, gap stats); ratios/shares/codes/one-hots/calendar untouched.
reasoning_summary: Dollar-scale features span 4 orders of magnitude; compressing them should reduce the influence of outliers and let the model fit the bulk of households better, which is what MAE rewards.

hypothesis: Campaign state at the snapshot matters, not just ever-targeted counts: households currently inside an active campaign window (esp. TypeA) and those targeted by a campaign starting in the last 28 days spend differently in the next 4 weeks than those whose campaigns ended weeks ago.
transformation_description: Added to E006: active-campaign count, active flags by type, days since most recent campaign start, days until nearest campaign end, started-in-28/84d flags, and interactions of active TypeA/B with trailing-28d spend.
reasoning_summary: E004 measured only cumulative targeting; campaign windows are short (~30 days), so the current active/just-started state is the more relevant exposure signal and should improve fit.

hypothesis: Where and how a household shops predicts its future spend: store diversity/loyalty, fine-grained commodity mix, basket-value variability, weekly spend CV, discount intensity per trip, and time-of-day patterns add signal beyond E006's level/trend/recency features.
transformation_description: Added to E006: store features (n_stores 7/28/84/364d, store-spend entropy, top-store share, 28d-vs-84d loyalty shift), top-15 commodity spend shares + commodity count/entropy (84d), basket stats (std/max/CV/max-share 84d, trips 7d, active days 28d), weekly CV & zero-share (26w), discount per trip (28d), morning/afternoon shares (84d).
reasoning_summary: Shopping patterns (store loyalty, what categories a household concentrates on, how variable its baskets are) are stable habits that should correlate with future spend level and volatility, which the level/trend features in E006 do not capture.

hypothesis: Basket-composition features (lines, basket size, unit price, product/dept counts, brand share, discount share, timing shares) add noise on top of the already-saturated spend/recency features; pruning them improves generalization.
transformation_description: Removed 13 basket-composition columns from E006's table (lines_84, lines_per_trip, avg_basket_84(+ts), unit_price_84, qty_28/84, national_share_84, n_products_84, n_depts_84, evening_share_84, weekend_share_84, disc_share_84), keeping the 99 spend/recency/zero-inflation/dept/campaign/demo/season features.
reasoning_summary: Ridge block-ablation on a day-431 temporal holdout showed dropping the basket block improves proxy MAE (67.39→67.02) while every other block helps; with the model saturated, correlated noise columns hurt.

hypothesis: Features that drift out of the training range at later snapshots (accumulating campaign counts, tenure/week indices, first-populating last-year windows, lifetime totals) act as spurious time-trend proxies the model can only extrapolate on and hurt validation MAE; removing them from E011 leaves stationary behavioural rates that transfer.
transformation_description: Dropped 19 drifting columns from E011: tenure, days_since_first, week, week_q, spend_ly, ly_trail28, ly_future28, total_spend, life_spend, all campaign counts/interactions (n_campaigns, camp_TypeA/B/C, camp_recent84, camp_x_demo, campA_x_spend28), redemp_total, days_since_redemp, z_active_wk_52.
reasoning_summary: Drift audit showed these features are 0.7–2.3 train-std away from their train means at validation and mostly out of range, yet correlate with the target on train, so the model extrapolates them; stationary spend-rate features carry the signal and should transfer better.

hypothesis: Spend is autocorrelated at the 4-week seasonal lag: rolling 4-week sums lagged by 13/14/26 weeks (same season last quarter/year) and household holiday-week spending share predict future_spend_4w beyond trailing windows; plus discount-mix and fine-grained department shares add signal.
transformation_description: E014 = E013 + 49 new features: hh-week spend matrix (26 wks) → rolling-4wk sums lag1..5,13,14,26 + ratios, weekly stats, holiday-week spend share/amount, market seasonal level, discount totals/shares (84d), 16 dept shares + entropy + n_depts (84d).
reasoning_summary: The 4-week-ahead target should correlate with spend in the same 4-week block of the previous quarter/year; a 26-week weekly matrix gives clean aligned lags. Discount share and fine department mix capture promo-driven and category-driven spend persistence that E013's coarse mix missed.

hypothesis: Long-window trailing features (spend_364, dec_112, z_dec_224, trips_364, z_zero_block_share, r_84_364) are biased early in training by window truncation (tenure ~90d at snap 95) but saturated at validation, creating a train/val semantic mismatch; tenure-normalized rates (weekly spend rate per available day, decayed-spend per decay-mass, trips per week) restore stationarity, and dropping out-of-range (week_cos shift 1.85σ) and near-zero-signal columns (redemp_84 97% NaN corr 0.02, homeowner/age/class3 codes, has_demo, trend, week encodings) reduces noise.
transformation_description: E015 = E013 minus 14 columns (week_sin/cos, trend, redemp_84, homeowner_code, age_code, class3_code, has_demo, z_dec_224, spend_364, trips_364, dec_112, z_zero_block_share, r_84_364) plus 6 tenure-normalized replacements: rate_112/182/364 (weekly spend per available day), trips_rate_364, dec112_rate (decayed spend per decay mass), tenure_cap364.
reasoning_summary: The dropped long-window features were the strongest drifters (drift 0.93-1.0) whose meaning changes between train and validation; their normalized replacements are stationary (rate_364 ~34-35 at every snapshot) and carry the same predictive signal (corr ~0.80-0.82), so the model sees consistent semantics across periods while removing pure-noise columns.

hypothesis: Exposure to in-store displays and weekly mailers predicts future spend: households whose recent purchases (28/84d) were of displayed/mailer-featured products, with current-week display/mailer coverage of their usual basket, and recent recency of exposure, buy more in the next 4 weeks.
transformation_description: E016 = E013 + 19 display/mailer exposure features: matched transaction lines to display_mailer (product x store x week) in last 28/84d giving exposed line counts, exposed spend and shares; weeks-since-last exposure; and current-week leading-indicator counts/shares of the household's 84d product set currently on display/mailer.
reasoning_summary: Display/mailer exposure is the last untapped table; exposed-line shares correlate 0.53 with future spend at snapshot 459, and current-week coverage of a household's habitual products is a plausible leading indicator of next-4-week trips.

hypothesis: Future 4-week spend mean-reverts toward the household's baseline: a recent spike (log recent spend minus log baseline) predicts LESS future spend than the raw recent level implies, so explicit log-scale spike/reversion features will improve on E013's raw ratios.
transformation_description: E017 = E013 + 8 log-scale spike features (log1p recent-window spend minus log1p scaled 84d baseline, windows 7/14/28/56d and decayed 28-vs-112d), pos/neg split of spike_28, and a damped rate feature d28*exp(-0.7*positive spike).
reasoning_summary: Diagnostics on train rows show a strong negative partial effect of the recent-vs-baseline spike on log target (-0.74) that raw ratio features only capture indirectly; explicit spike features let the model apply reversion directly.

hypothesis: The fixed model under-fits the heavy right tail (top decile: y 569 vs pred 431) and the zero floor (y≈0 rows get pred ~32); residual correlations are ~0, so the gap is nonlinearity, not new linear features. Hinge (piecewise-linear) expansions of the strongest spend predictors let the model fit tail slopes and the zero floor separately.

hypothesis: Promotional-discount engagement and shopping rhythm predict future spend beyond E013's behavioral history: coupon/loyalty discount dollars and rates (28/84/364d), share of discounted lines and trips, day-of-week trip entropy/top-day share, morning/evening time-of-day shares, time-of-day variability, bulk-buying (max quantity, ≥6-unit share, units per trip).
transformation_description: E019 = E013 + 15 new features (discount engagement 5, shopping rhythm 7, basket size/quantity 3), joined onto the E013 table per snapshot.
reasoning_summary: Discount-seeking and regular shopping rhythms are stable household traits that signal engagement level and planned stock-up behavior; none of E013's features capture promotion sensitivity or weekly timing, so they should add independent signal.
